extracted.intended_audience: salt-makers, miners, and natural philosophers / Royal Society readers
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed seventeenth-century procedural guidance and empirical observations for producing and grading salt (and related notes on quicksilver production), including pan design, mixtures, boiling regimen, yields, and finishing methods. Aimed at practitioners and scientific observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brine-to-salt yield measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative method to determine how much salt a given volume/weight of brine yields (example conclusion: 'yields one pound of salt for six pounds of brine').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh a quart mark by filling a narrow-mouthed bottle with distilled water; fill to same mark with brine and weigh (examples: one sample weighed two pounds three ounces five drachms and boiled to 5 ounces 2 drachms salt; another weighed two pounds four ounces one drachm and boiled to 6 ounces 6 drachms 2 scruples). Boil away brine without addition/clarification to obtain salt weight. Use repeated measures to detect effects of pit drawing and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of pit drawing and tides on brine strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational observation/criterion about what affects brine strength: heavy drawing of the pit quickens inflow of salt springs and strengthens brine; spring-tides are not a reliable cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare brine taken when pit 'had only begun to work' to brine taken after the pit 'had been drawn' several days; the latter yielded noticeably more salt. Conclude increased drawing allows salt-springs to come quicker and reduces admission of fresh springs; therefore strength varies with drawing, not necessarily with tidal phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pans design and material
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification of pans historically used and their proportions: six leaden pans → four iron-pans → two greater pans; typical iron-pan near four feet breadth and length, sides about six inches deep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pans are set upon iron-bars, bricked in very close. When four pans used in one house the pans' content is gauged to former 'six leads' proportion. Fig. references give model dimensions. Choice of pan size affects boiling time and final salt characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel and furnace arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of pit-coals (from Staffordshire) and pan setting on iron bars bricked close; hot-house built by two tunnels under the pans conveying smoke to chimney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pans set upon iron bars bricked close; hot-house located behind works, made by two tunnels under pans; partition walls and hearth arrangements described (figures referenced). Boards/plaster may not withstand steam/condensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of clarifying agents and scum removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific mixtures (blood and 'whites') as aids during boiling to bring up scum for removal: initial 'blood' mixture at first boil, then 'whites' (egg white mixed with brine) at refill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare 'blood' mixture: ~20 gallons brine + 2 quarts calves/cows/sheep's blood, add ~2 quarts to a pan of ~360 quarts to produce a scum to skim. At refill use 'whites' made of a quart of egg whites beaten with brine, mixed into 20 gallons and add ~2 quarts; boil sharply until second scum arises and skim it off. Continue gentle boiling until 'corne' appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling regimen and timing to maximize yield and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence and intensity of heat during the operation: quick fire at first until half brine wasted ('boiling upon the fresh'), refill and sharper boil for second scum, then gentle boiling until grain forms; avoid fast boiling late in process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workmen assert that boiling fast in later stages 'wastes their salt.' Add a small quantity (~a quarter of a pint per pan) of strong ale when part of brine is wasted to produce a momentary ebullition, then abate fire to maintain a gentle boil. Continue gentle boiling until a thin 'scum like ice' (first appearance of salt) forms and grains gather on bottom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of pan size and handling on grain, clarity, and durability
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller, shallower pans: work done in ~2 hours; salt 'weighs heavier' and melts less but granulates less. Greater, deeper pans: take ~half hour longer; produce clearer, better-granulated salt that is apt to melt in moist air unless grains are larger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller pans generally boil more brine away and produce heavier, longer-lasting salt though less granular. Larger pans remove salt from brine earlier and only harden in hot-house leading to clearer granulation but greater tendency to melt; larger grain size increases durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granulation causation (timing vs additives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of what causes salt granulation: removal of salt from brine before it is wasted is likely the cause of granulation rather than addition of ale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workmen attribute granulation to ale; author believes taking salt out of brine before waste causes granulation more than the ale addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling and finishing: loots, barrows, draining and hot-house hardening
rubrics_metrics.description: Method for collecting, draining and hardening salt: rake with loots, place into flat cleft wicker 'barrows' (sugar-loaf shape, bottom uppermost), let drain ~1.5 hours in leach-trough, then move to hot-house (tunnels under pans) to harden; leach brine reused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect salt with loots until little brine left; lift into barrows allowing brine to drop; when barrow full let it stand ~an hour and a half in trough to drain, then move to hot-house. Leach brine from barrows is returned to next boiling as it is salt melted and only needs hardening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of salt and finishing distinctions (cats vs loaves; white vs gray)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and manufacturing distinctions: 'white' salt is fine table salt; 'gray' salt is sweepings; 'cats' are worst salt moulded and baked for pigeon-houses; 'loaves' are finest and prepared/tamped and baked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cats of salt: made of worst salt when still wet, mixed with cummin-seed and ashes, baked into hard lumps for pigeon-houses. Loaves of salt: cut the barrows intended for loaves with a long slit both sides, tie sides together, fill and ram down salt, place promptly in hot-house, then untie and bake in ovens after the bread is drawn; repeat till firm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality criterion for salt as preservative
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical test of salt quality: efficacy in preserving meat (beef and bacon) for long periods and degree of penetration ('more salt to the midst').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author reports Cheshire salt preserves beef and bacon 'very well' a whole year and seems 'more searching' (penetrating) than French salt based on consumption experience; shipments of Cheshire bacon to London show no infamy—use preservation efficacy as a quality metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pan covering and workshop ventilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational rule: pans are never covered during boiling; houses are open to the thatch with vent-holes to allow steam escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pans kept uncovered during boiling; houses resemble barns open to the thatch with one or two cover-holes to vent steam. Plaster won't stick and boards warp due to steam; tiles possibly better but untried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement protocol and experimental controls for brine observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Protocol for controlled measurement of brine properties and yield using identical quart marks and repeated trials to compare samples over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same bottle/quart mark filled with distilled water as reference; fill with brine samples taken at different times/conditions and weigh to compare; boil identically without additions to compare salt yields; note pit drawing state and time relative to tides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reuse and economy of leach brine
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural standard: leach brine drained from barrows is to be returned to the next boiling because it is 'salt melted' and only needs hardening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect leach brine in trough; put it into the next boiling to increase economy of salt recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of quicksilver types (virgin vs plain) and extraction criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of quicksilver: 'virgin' (lungāraw) that appears without fire (visible in ore or flows as drops/streams) vs 'plain' quicksilver which requires fire to be forced out of cinnabar/ore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virgin quicksilver: either visible directly in ore or liberated by washing/separation (sieving and troughs). Plain quicksilver: not visible initially and obtained by distillation/separation by fire in iron furnaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ore processing and separation methods for mercury
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred procedure: powder the best (hard-stone) ore, sieve to separate any virgin mercury; material not passing sieve is submitted to fire in iron furnaces for distillation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best ore is a hard stone; powder grossly and work by sieve to separate virgin mercury; residue processed in iron furnaces (50 retorts per furnace, 800 retorts and as many recipients working in sets as described). Numbers of retorts, furnaces and handling described as industrial-scale guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quicksilver production logistics and packaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational/commerce details and metrics: production volumes, packaging, and transport units (saumes of ~315 lb), storage in double leather, retort costs noted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example outputs: 40 saumes carried out (each 315 lb) valued at 400 ducats of gold; castle stores 3000 saumes in barrels; retorts available in large quantities (heap of ~16,000 iron retorts) and each retort costs about a crown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health hazard note for mercury miners
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that mercury getting into workers' bodies causes languishing destruction; workmen are injured by mercury though not necessarily suddenly suffocated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of chronic mercury poisoning risks in quicksilver mines; the text reports workers 'languishingly destroyed' by mercury exposure.
